questions.stem: Approximately how many alveoli form one lobule of the breast?
questions.explanation: The slide states that about 10 to 100 alveoli form one lobule.
questions.sourceEvidence: The slide specifies approximately 10–100 alveoli per lobule.

questions.stem: Approximately how many lobules form one breast lobe?
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a range of 20 to 40 lobules per lobe.
questions.sourceEvidence: The slide states that 20–40 lobules form one lobe.

questions.stem: Which statement about the breast's capsule is consistent with the lecture?
options: It is enclosed by a thick fibrous capsule
It has no capsule and is embedded in fatty tissue
It is enclosed by a synovial capsule
It has a capsule only around the ducts
questions.explanation: The slide notes that the breast has no capsule and is embedded in fatty tissue.
questions.sourceEvidence: The note explicitly says the breast has no capsule and is embedded in fatty tissue.

questions.stem: In which direction is the nipple typically directed?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes the nipple as directed downward and outward.
questions.sourceEvidence: The slide's note states the nipple is directed downward and outward.

questions.stem: In a large breast, how may the usual nipple position relative to the fourth intercostal space change?
options: It remains at the same level in all cases
questions.explanation: The slide notes that the nipple may be lower in a large breast.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states the nipple is opposite the fourth intercostal space but is lower if the breast is large.

questions.stem: What is the approximate distance of the nipple from the midline described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The slide gives an approximate distance of four inches from the midline.
questions.sourceEvidence: The nipple landmark is stated as four inches from the midline.

questions.stem: Which breast-skin region drains to the apical group of lymph nodes, excluding the nipple and areola?
questions.explanation: The skin of the upper quadrants drains to the apical lymph-node group.
questions.sourceEvidence: The skin-drainage list assigns upper quadrants to apical nodes.

questions.stem: Where does lymph from the skin of the lower breast quadrants (excluding nipple and areola) drain according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lower-quadrant skin drains to the lymph plexus of the rectus sheath and the subphrenic plexus.
questions.sourceEvidence: The stated drainage routes for lower-quadrant skin are rectus sheath and subphrenic plexuses.

questions.stem: Which lymphatic connection is described for some lymphatics from the medial breast?
options: They cross the sternum to anastomose with the opposite breast
They pass directly to the deep cervical nodes
They join the portal venous system
They cross the diaphragm to the liver
questions.explanation: Some medial lymphatics cross the front of the sternum and communicate with the opposite breast.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text describes intermammary lymphatics crossing anterior to the sternum to the opposite breast.

questions.stem: A small proportion of lymph from breast tissue is described as draining to which nodes?
questions.explanation: The lecture assigns about 5% of breast-tissue lymph to paravertebral, posterior intercostal nodes.
questions.sourceEvidence: The drainage proportions list 5% to paravertebral (posterior intercostal) nodes.

questions.stem: Which arterial source contributes perforating branches to the breast?
questions.explanation: Perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery are listed among the breast's arterial supply.
questions.sourceEvidence: The blood-supply list names perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery.

questions.stem: From which range of intercostal arteries do branches supplying the breast arise?
questions.explanation: The slide specifies anterior and posterior intercostal branches from the second through fifth intercostal arteries.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text specifies the second to fifth intercostal arteries.

questions.stem: According to the breast arterial-source table, which artery supplies the medial part (about 30%)?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic artery is listed as supplying the medial part, about 30%.
questions.sourceEvidence: The table pairs internal thoracic artery with medial part (30%).

questions.stem: Which arteries are listed as supplying the upper part of the breast (about 1–5%)?
questions.explanation: The table assigns the upper part (about 1–5%) to thoracoacromial and superior thoracic arteries.
questions.sourceEvidence: The arterial table lists thoracoacromial and superior thoracic arteries for upper part (1–5%).

questions.stem: According to the lecture, how far does the male breast duct system extend?
options: To the margin of the areola, without extending beyond it
Only to the nipple, with no ducts beneath the areola
questions.explanation: The slide describes the male duct system as embedded in connective tissue and not extending beyond the areolar margin.
questions.sourceEvidence: The slide says the male duct system does not extend beyond the margin of the areola.

questions.stem: Which venous feature provides a route by which breast cancer may spread to vertebrae?
options: Valveless veins connecting with the vertebral venous plexus
Valved veins draining to the pulmonary veins
questions.explanation: The slides note valveless veins connect the breast to the vertebral venous plexus, enabling spread to vertebrae.
questions.sourceEvidence: The note links valveless veins to the vertebral venous plexus with possible vertebral spread.
